Thanks Mina/Kim —

Quick clarifying questions from our performance team as we evaluate the RFP artifacts you provided:

1) Prefill / prefetch behavior: can you briefly describe how you populate KV cache and prefix cache for model-serving workloads when an endpoint sees a sudden sustained QPS (e.g., 800–1,200 QPS sustained for 30+ minutes)? Is that an active prefetch step during rollout or purely reactive warming from live traffic?

2) Tail-latency under sustained load: your summary sheet lists 99th percentile numbers but not the full test methodology. Were those 99p numbers from steady-state runs after warmup, or include cold-starts and transient spikes? Please indicate sequence length distributions used (token counts) and model variant/quantization used in those runs.

3) Reproducibility: what artifacts can you share for us to independently validate — raw latency histograms, qps/time series, and the synthetic driver configuration (seeded prompts, concurrency profile)?

We'd appreciate a concise reply and any attachments you can share. If useful, we can schedule a 30-minute deep-dive with our perf engineers.

Subject: Re: RFP Q: prefetch/KV cache population and sustained QPS validation

Hi Sarah —

Thanks for the clear questions. Attached is a short explainer (redwood-prefetch-kvcache-explainer.pdf) and a condensed CSV summary (vs-benchmark-summary-20270809.csv). High level answers below; happy to walk through details in a session.

1) Prefill / KV-cache behavior (short):
- For production endpoints we support two mechanisms: an opt-in active prefill job at rollout time, and an automatic reactive warmup that leverages continuous batching + prefix prefetch.
- Active prefill: customers can provide representative prompt prefixes (or Redwood can sample from a safe prompt set) and we run a controlled async prefill across replicas to populate KV caches and per-replica prefix caches before traffic is routed broadly. This is typically used for canary→full rollout flows where tail-latency during ramp is critical.
- Reactive warmup: when traffic increases, our serving runtime uses short-lived high-concurrency bursts to populate KV and prefix caches within seconds; this leverages our KV-merging logic so multiple concurrent requests that share prefixes reuse cache entries rather than duplicating work.
- Operational controls: you can set a prefill budget (tokens/replica), max parallelism, and canary window. We also expose prefill progress and cache-hit metrics in the Console.

2) Tail-latency and methodology (short):
- The 99th percentile numbers in the sheet are steady-state, post-warmup results. Each reported run had a 10-minute warmup phase (gradual ramp from 0 to target QPS), then a 30-minute steady-state window during which we collected histograms. We excluded outliers from transient infra events per the documented filtering rules in the explainer.
- Typical test parameters included: target QPS: 800 / 1,000 / 1,200; concurrency per worker tuned to saturate GPU batch sizes; sequence length distributions: 8–32 tokens (60%), 33–128 (30%), 129–512 (10%) for the conversational use case you provided. Model used: open-RW-13B v2 (FP16) and quantized int8 variant for cost-sensitive runs.
- Example numbers from the CSV (steady-state post-warmup):
  * 800 QPS, RW-13B FP16: p50 24ms, p95 62ms, p99 115ms
  * 1,200 QPS, RW-13B int8: p50 28ms, p95 78ms, p99 156ms
- Cold starts: we measure cold-starts separately. Cold-start tail depends on model size and whether an active prefill was used; without prefill, cold-start p99 can be several seconds for large models unless an autoscaler pre-provisions replicas.

3) Reproducibility / artifacts we can provide:
- We can share: full latency histograms (per-second), raw qps/time-series, synthetic driver config and seed prompt set, and the exact harness commands used (k6 + our load-proxy). For sensitive artifacts we provide a time-limited S3 snapshot and a readme describing the run steps.

Attachments included: redwood-prefetch-kvcache-explainer.pdf, vs-benchmark-summary-20270809.csv

Next steps: if you want the S3 snapshot we can stage it and share a link; otherwise we can schedule a 30-minute walkthrough with our perf engineering and the test harness owner (Karthik).

Best,

Mina Haddad
Head of Product — Performance
Redwood Inference

Mina —

Appreciate the quick and thorough reply. A couple of follow-ups from our bench team before we schedule the deep-dive:

A) For reproducibility we need the following as discrete artifacts so our SREs can re-run on our side:
  - raw latency histograms (per-second) for the full 30-minute steady window
  - the exact load-driver config (k6 script / YAML) and random seed used
  - the input prompt set (anonymized) used for prefill and steady runs

B) Acceptance criteria we intend to run:
  - run the same harness against a Redwood-provided snapshot and our in-house replay; acceptable margin: +/- 10% on p95 and +/- 20% on p99 for steady-state windows
  - a documented DoD that includes warmup steps, cache-prefill parameterization, and whether autoscaling policies were enabled

C) Can you confirm whether the CSV numbers include network transit time to our region (we'll be running in us-west-2) or are they service-only (request entering the platform to token emission)?

If you can stage the artifacts to an S3 path and share a short readme, we can kick off the re-run this week.

Thanks — look forward to the link.

—Sarah
